Curriculum Learning Teaches LLMs Long-Horizon Implicit Reasoning, Up To A Limit

Jimson Huang ††thanks: Equal contribution.    Maxwell Nickell11footnotemark: 1    Ruowang Zhang    Abulhair Saparov Affiliation: Purdue University Affiliation: West Lafayette, IN 47907, USA Affiliation: {huan2073, mnickel, zhan5763, asaparov}@purdue.edu
Abstract

LLMs “reason” by externalizing intermediate steps as tokens through chain-of-thought (CoT), yet even frontier reasoning models hit abrupt performance cliffs on long-horizon tasks. Implicit reasoning—reasoning within a single forward pass—is useful during CoT generation, as the model can “search ahead” to decide the correct next move without explicit search. Models with weak implicit reasoning are more likely to commit to wrong paths and must attempt to recover via backtracking, while models with strong implicit reasoning identify the correct proof strategy directly, shortening the CoT. However, prior work shows LLMs struggle to reason implicitly beyond shallow depths, with no relief from scale. We investigate whether curriculum learning can extend this depth by fine-tuning on examples with progressively increasing vocabulary size and lookahead—the number of steps a model must search ahead to identify the correct next move. At matched compute, curriculum-trained models achieve lookaheads where no-curriculum training fails—Qwen3-0.6B reaches 98%98\% accuracy on problems with lookahead up to 256256 with curriculum, compared to 45%45\% without. However, progress slows as fine-tuning continues, following a saturating exponential that suggests a maximum intrinsic lookahead to which models can learn to reason implicitly. Larger models reach higher fitted ceilings, fine-tuning pretrained models far outpaces training from scratch, and curriculum step sizes that are too large stall progression. Finally, the capability acquired on synthetic data transfers to natural language reasoning, with curriculum-trained models outperforming models trained without curriculum at matched compute on 1111 natural language reasoning benchmarks.

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied in reasoning-intensive settings such as coding (Jimenez et al., 2024), deductive proof generation (Polu and Sutskever, 2020), planning (Valmeekam et al., 2023), multi-hop question answering (Yang et al., 2018), and game AI (Silver et al., 2018). Reasoning in LLMs is typically performed by externalizing intermediate tokens through chain-of-thought (Wei et al., 2022, CoT;), and reinforcement learning has been used to further improve reasoning performance (Jaech et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025). However, even state-of-the-art reasoning models struggle on long-horizon tasks, hitting abrupt performance cliffs at modest depths, and these failures persist even when models are given their full reasoning-token budgets (Rameshkumar et al., 2025). Errors early in a reasoning chain can compound over the remaining steps (Dziri et al., 2023), forcing models to spend substantial tokens backtracking in order to recover. Even when models avoid such mistakes, reasoning chains can consume a considerable amount of tokens when each reasoning step makes only a small advance towards the solution.

Implicit reasoning occurs within a single forward pass and determines how far a model can “look ahead” over potential later steps before committing to the next CoT step. This capability becomes increasingly important in long-horizon reasoning tasks, which require the model to reason over greater depths. Consider the example in Figure 1, where a model with weak implicit reasoning commits to a wrong path and must attempt to recover via backtracking, while a model with strong implicit reasoning looks far enough ahead to identify the correct next step directly, shortening the CoT. Despite these benefits, recent work has shown that transformers struggle to learn implicit search beyond shallow depths, with no relief from increased model scale (Saparov et al., 2025). This raises the question: can LLMs be trained to perform long-horizon implicit reasoning, and if so, is there a limit to the depth they can reach?

To address this question, we examine whether the training procedure itself can be shaped to unlock deeper implicit reasoning. Incrementally increasing the depth a model must look ahead during training might offer a natural path to do so, and we therefore investigate whether curriculum learning (Bengio et al., 2009) can extend this depth. We generate training data using a modified version of DeepRD (Rameshkumar et al., 2025), where each example provides a set of premises in natural language over entities and attributes (e.g., in “Alex is a cat,” “Alex” is an entity and “cat” is an attribute) and asks the model to predict the next step of a multi-hop proof. We deliberately keep the curriculum simple, as our goal is not to find the optimal design but to characterize the behavior of curriculum training itself. Our curriculum gradually increases the lookahead—the number of steps a model must search ahead to identify the correct next step—jointly with the attribute vocabulary, which we find outperforms a curriculum over lookahead alone (Section 4.1). As an illustration, the lookahead in Figure 1 is 3, since the model must search 3 steps ahead to conclude that the correct second step is “Carol is Bob’s mother,” and not “George is Bob’s father.” By training only on the output of a single forward pass, we isolate implicit reasoning as a pure computational capability, separating it from what can be achieved by externalizing intermediate steps. With this setup, we pose two primary research questions. RQ1: Can LLMs learn to reason implicitly to arbitrary depths, and what training conditions—including curriculum, model size, and initialization—govern this capability? RQ2: Does training a model to perform long-horizon implicit reasoning improve its performance on downstream natural-language reasoning tasks?

We make the following contributions to answer the aforementioned research questions:

  1. C1

    We introduce a curriculum over lookahead and attribute vocabulary and show that it extends the depth to which LLMs can reason implicitly. At matched compute, Qwen3-0.6B reaches 98%98\% accuracy on problems up to lookahead 256256 with curriculum vs. 45%45\% without (Section 4.1).

  2. C2

    We show that achieved lookahead grows predictably with training compute, following a saturating exponential, suggesting a maximum intrinsic lookahead to which each model can learn to reason implicitly (Section 4.2).

  3. C3

    We show that larger models have higher maximum intrinsic lookaheads, that pretrained initialization allows a model to reason implicitly to far greater depths than training from scratch, and that the curriculum step size (the increase in lookahead between successive stages) must be small enough for training to progress. Pythia-410M, 1.4B, and 2.8B have maximum intrinsic lookaheads of 5151, 8282, and 235235, respectively (Section 4.4). At a 1.51.5M PFLOP budget, Pythia-1.4B achieves lookahead 6363 from pretrained weights vs. 2323 from random initialization (Section 4.5). With Qwen3-0.6B, step size 6464 stalls at lookahead 128128, while step size 88 reaches 256256 (Section 4.3).

  4. C4

    We show that the implicit reasoning capability acquired on synthetic data transfers to natural language reasoning. Curriculum-trained models outperform models trained without curriculum at matched compute on 1111 benchmarks, with the largest gains on multi-step deductive reasoning—Qwen3-1.7B gains 14.314.3 points on ProofWriter OWA at lookahead 4848 (Section 4.6).

2 Related Work

Reasoning and search in transformers.

A growing line of work characterizes how LLMs struggle in long-horizon reasoning. Dziri et al. (2023) argue that transformers reduce multi-step reasoning to pattern matching, so errors compound as tasks grow more complex. Formal analyses of deductive reasoning show that LLMs reason greedily at branch points (Saparov and He, 2023) and that their accuracy decreases as the correct proof grows longer (Saparov et al., 2023). Saparov et al. (2025) formalize task complexity via a lookahead metric and show that while small transformers can learn to search under a carefully balanced training distribution, learning degrades as graphs grow, with no relief from model scale. Rameshkumar et al. (2025) show that even frontier reasoning models hit a performance cliff at modest lookaheads on graph connectivity and proof planning, without exhausting their token budgets. Heyman and Zylberberg (2025) report similar failures on graph-coloring tasks.

Explicit and implicit reasoning.

Explicit reasoning externalizes tokens via CoT prompting (Wei et al., 2022) and its derivatives (Wang et al., 2023b; Yao et al., 2023), extended further by trace-supervised search (Lehnert et al., 2024; Gandhi et al., 2024) and reinforcement learning (Lambert et al., 2024; Jaech et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025). Implicit approaches enhance reasoning without verbalizing intermediate steps via learnable auxiliary tokens (Goyal et al., 2024), soft tokens in place of discrete tokens (Hao et al., 2025; Shen et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2026), or architectural recurrence (Dehghani et al., 2019; Geiping et al., 2025). Mechanistic studies show transformers can reason implicitly within a forward pass (Brinkmann et al., 2024; Jenner et al., 2024), and it can emerge through grokking, but only with significant over-training (Wang et al., 2024). However, implicit reasoning can reflect shortcut learning rather than generalizable reasoning (Lin et al., 2025b), and its generalization depends on which compositional structures appear in training (Ye et al., 2025).

Curriculum learning for reasoning.

In early curriculum learning work, Bengio et al. (2009) train language models on a restricted vocabulary that is progressively expanded; our attribute-vocabulary curriculum applies the same idea to the attributes of synthetic proofs. Curriculum learning has since been used to improve performance on reasoning tasks, for example by gradually removing CoT tokens (Deng et al., 2024) or replacing them with soft tokens (Hao et al., 2025) while keeping the remainder of the prompt invariant. Our curriculum instead never uses CoT and increases the lookahead of the problems. Recent theoretical results show that staged curricula can avoid exponential sample-complexity bottlenecks (Wang et al., 2025; Bu et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026) and can enable agents trained with reinforcement learning to perform search on trees that are deeper than those seen during training (Yang et al., 2026). Empirically, the picture is mixed: curriculum learning improves learning efficiency (Abbe et al., 2024) and mitigates, but does not eliminate, the exponential data cost of implicit kk-hop reasoning in small from-scratch models (Yao et al., 2025), while difficulty-ordering a fixed dataset gives no robust advantage for explicit CoT post-training (Mordig et al., 2026). Lee et al. (2025) report that pretrained initialization accelerates curriculum progression. Whether a curriculum can unlock implicit reasoning in pretrained LLMs at depths where direct training fails has remained open; our work answers this question.

3 Methods

3.1 Task Formulation and Complexity

We study whether LLMs can learn to perform long-horizon reasoning implicitly, where the model emits the next proof step directly, without intermediate reasoning tokens. To do so, we focus on the task of predicting the next step in a proof: given a set of premises and a goal conclusion, the model must identify the correct next step in a valid proof of the goal from the premises. A proof is a sequence of proof steps, where each proof step has some premises followed by a conclusion, and the conclusion of one proof step may serve as a premise for a later proof step. Solving the task requires the model to search through possible inference paths, starting from the premises, and find a proof from the premises to the goal.

Training Data.

To generate examples of this task, we use a modified version of the DeepRD dataset. In DeepRD, each problem is generated by first generating a directed acyclic graph (DAG). Each graph is then translated into natural language by mapping every node into an atomic proposition (e.g., “Alice is a cat”) and every edge into a rule (e.g., “If Alice is a cat, then Alice is a mammal”). In DeepRD, attribute names, such as “cat”, are replaced with fictional names (e.g., “zorbi”) to facilitate the generation of very large reasoning problems and to avoid data contamination issues during evaluation. Since DeepRD is synthetic, we can generate a limitless number of examples for large-scale training. Some examples are shown in Appendix H. A key reason we choose DeepRD is that our curriculum requires a large number of examples whose lookahead is highly controllable and can be made arbitrarily large. Real-world reasoning data cannot meet this requirement, because its complexity is long-tailed (Rameshkumar et al., 2025) and examples with very large lookahead are rare. The representation of each reasoning problem as a graph enables us to precisely control problem complexity: in the graph analogy, finding a proof from a premise to a goal is equivalent to finding a directed path from a start node to a goal node.

Lookahead.

We measure task complexity using the lookahead ℓ\ell which is the minimum number of breadth-first search iterations that must be performed from the start node to determine the correct next step in the path to the goal. Intuitively, ℓ\ell captures how far the model must search to determine the correct path from incorrect alternatives.11 1 For a formal definition, see Rameshkumar et al. (2025); Saparov et al. (2025). This is distinct from the length of the path from the start node to the goal node. For example, if the start node has only one valid child node, no search is needed to determine the next correct step, regardless of the distance of the goal node from the start node. In this case, ℓ=1\ell=1, and lookahead is a more faithful characterization of problem complexity.

3.2 Curriculum over Lookahead and Attribute Vocabulary

We aim to test whether curriculum learning can help transformers to learn to perform long-horizon implicit reasoning. With this in mind, we develop a curriculum learning procedure (Figure 8 and Algorithm 1, Appendix A). We train the model in stages: at stage kk, the model is presented with examples whose lookahead is at most LkL_{k}, where Lk=k⋅sL_{k}=k\cdot s and s≥1s\geq 1 is the curriculum step size—i.e., the amount by which the lookahead is increased at each stage of the curriculum. For example, with s=8s=8, a 12-stage curriculum advances through Lk=8,16,24,…,96L_{k}=8,16,24,\ldots,96. Figure 13 illustrates the first three stages of a curriculum with s=1s=1. At each stage, we perform supervised fine-tuning on examples from DeepRD where, for each example ii, the lookahead of the example ℓi\ell_{i} is sampled i.i.d. from a uniform distribution ℓi∼Uniform​{1,…,Lk}\ell_{i}\sim\text{Uniform}\{1,\ldots,L_{k}\}. Including easier examples at each stage helps prevent catastrophic forgetting of previously learned lookaheads. The training objective is cross-entropy on the answer tokens: the tokens identifying the correct next attribute in the proof chain. The model advances from stage kk to stage k+1k+1 when its exact-match accuracy over the most recent WW training examples reaches 98%.

Attribute-vocabulary curriculum.

Besides lookahead, the number of distinct attribute labels that appear across training examples also affects the difficulty of the task. We therefore also grow the attribute vocabulary as part of the curriculum, akin to the vocabulary curriculum of Bengio et al. (2009). The attributes in each generated proof are given fictional labels (e.g., zorbi in “Alice is zorbi”); the attribute vocabulary 𝒱k\mathcal{V}_{k} is the pool of these attribute labels available to the instances at stage kk, and |𝒱k||\mathcal{V}_{k}| denotes its size. We emphasize that |𝒱k||\mathcal{V}_{k}| does not refer to the model’s tokenizer vocabulary. The tokenizer and its token set are unchanged, and each attribute label is encoded as ordinary subword tokens. We grow |𝒱k||\mathcal{V}_{k}| with lookahead LkL_{k} so that the vocabulary is always sufficient to provide distinct attributes with distinct labels. Specifically, an instance at lookahead LkL_{k} contains at most 2​Lk+12L_{k}+1 distinct attributes: the “correct chain” of length LkL_{k} plus a distractor chain of length LkL_{k} that shares the initial attribute as the correct chain. We set |𝒱k|=2​(Lk+1)|\mathcal{V}_{k}|=2(L_{k}+1), which is one more than the upper bound, so every attribute in each instance can receive a distinct label. A pool smaller than 2​Lk+12L_{k}+1 would force two or more attributes to share a label, which would make the problem ill-posed. We explore whether this joint curriculum over both lookahead and attribute vocabulary size performs better than a curriculum over lookahead alone (Section 4.1). In the latter setting, holding the pool fixed at its maximum size from the start leaves proof structure unchanged and only reduces cross-instance reuse of attribute labels.

4 Experiments and Results

Models.

We use two model families. Qwen3 (Yang et al., 2025, 0.6B, 1.7B;) gives capable models at low training cost across our many curriculum configurations, and it has fairly strong instruction following capabilities, which facilitates evaluation using downstream benchmarks that require specifically formatted outputs (Section 4.6). Pythia (Biderman et al., 2023, 160M, 410M, 1.4B, 2.8B;) provides models of different sizes pretrained, where each model is trained on the same data and the same number of tokens, so that they differ mainly in scale, together with base (non-instruction-tuned) checkpoints; our scaling and initialization comparisons (Sections 4.4 and 4.5) rely on both properties.

Setup.

All training examples are generated with our modified DeepRD generator as described in Sections 3.1 and 3.2. Experiments perform full fine-tuning with AdamW, a constant learning rate, and bf16 precision; per-experiment hyperparameters are listed in Appendix B. Training compute is estimated as C≈6​N​DC\approx 6ND (Kaplan et al., 2020, NN parameters, DD tokens;).

Evaluation.

The comparison of training with vs. without curriculum (Section 4.1) uses exact-match accuracy of the predicted next attribute on a held-out set shared by both settings, with lookaheads sampled uniformly from 1 to LL (Appendix E).22 2 While using curriculum learning, the maximum lookahead of samples reaches LL only at the final stage. All other synthetic-task experiments report achieved lookahead LL, the last curriculum stage completed, i.e., the largest LL at which the rolling exact-match training accuracy reaches 98%98\% (Section 3.2).

Baselines.

In both the next-step proof prediction comparisons (Section 4.1) and the downstream transfer experiments (Section 4.6), the baseline is the same model trained without curriculum, directly on data with a fixed maximum lookahead LL from the start, compared against its curriculum-trained counterpart at matched training compute.

4.1 Curriculum Learning Enables Deeper Reasoning at Matched Compute

Curriculum versus no curriculum. To determine whether curriculum learning is needed to train models to perform long-horizon reasoning implicitly, we compare training Qwen3-0.6B with curriculum learning at s=8s=8 against training without curriculum learning, where the maximum lookahead is fixed from the start. We run this comparison for each maximum lookahead L∈{96,104,112,120,128,256}L\in\{96,104,112,120,128,256\}. Figure 2 shows evaluation accuracy vs. cumulative training compute for L∈{96,128,256}L\in\{96,128,256\}, with the full sweep reported in Appendix C.1.

Table 1 summarizes the compute required to reach 98%98\% evaluation accuracy across all six values of LL. For L≤128L\leq 128 both methods eventually converge, but training with curriculum is consistently 1.251.25–2.27×2.27\times more compute-efficient. At maximum lookahead L=256L{=}256 the gap becomes qualitative: training without curriculum plateaus at ∼\sim45% accuracy and never converges within the compute budget, while training with curriculum continues climbing to 98%98\%.

Joint curriculum over attribute vocabulary. We next test the design choice introduced in Section 3.2: using a curriculum over both attribute vocabulary size and lookahead, with |𝒱k|=2​(Lk+1)|\mathcal{V}_{k}|=2(L_{k}+1), versus using a curriculum over lookahead alone, with the attribute vocabulary fixed at its maximum size throughout training. We train Qwen3-0.6B under both configurations, holding all other hyperparameters constant. Figure 3 and Table 9 show that the joint curriculum completes L=128L{=}128 within 100100K PFLOPs, where the fixed-vocabulary configuration has completed only L=96L{=}96. One plausible explanation is the following: at a fixed (large) attribute vocabulary, the model sees fewer examples of each attribute label in diverse reasoning contexts, encouraging memorization rather than generalization, while the joint curriculum keeps the attribute vocabulary small in early stages and grows it progressively as the model masters larger lookaheads. We therefore conduct all subsequent experiments using the joint curriculum over lookahead and attribute vocabulary size.

Vocabulary growth rate. Beyond whether to grow the attribute vocabulary at all, we also test how quickly it should grow. We compare |𝒱k|=b​Lk+2|\mathcal{V}_{k}|=bL_{k}+2 for b∈{2,3,4}b\in\{2,3,4\} on Qwen3-0.6B with s=8s=8 under an otherwise identical curriculum (Figure 3). At b=2b=2, this recovers our original schedule, |𝒱k|=2​Lk+2=2​(Lk+1)|\mathcal{V}_{k}|=2L_{k}+2=2(L_{k}+1). For a given lookahead, a larger bb “widens” the deepest instances from 22 branches to bb, rather than simply enlarging the attribute vocabulary while holding proof structure fixed, since |𝒱k||\mathcal{V}_{k}| is one more than the maximum number of attributes in an instance. This comparison therefore varies proof breadth alongside attribute vocabulary size. Within a budget of 100K PFLOPs, the three settings achieve L=128L{=}128, 7272, and 6464, respectively. Thus, the curriculum design that advances fastest is the one that grows the attribute vocabulary while holding the deepest instances at two branches (b=2b=2), and we use this configuration in all subsequent experiments.

4.2 Achieved Lookahead Grows Predictably toward an Apparent Ceiling

Having shown that curriculum is instrumental in teaching models to perform long-horizon implicit reasoning, we examine how achieved lookahead grows with compute. Figure 4 plots achieved LL against cumulative training compute (PFLOPs, log–log) for the trajectories of two models trained under our curriculum with s=1s=1: Qwen3-0.6B and Pythia-1.4B. In both cases achieved LL grows smoothly with compute but decelerates, curving below a straight line on log--log axes. We fit two functional forms33 3 We also fit a shifted power law, L=a​(C+Cs)pL=a(C+C_{s})^{p}, and a saturating power law, L=L∞−b​C−kL=L_{\infty}-bC^{-k}. The fitted shift CsC_{s} is close to zero, so the fitted function is effectively equivalent to a plain power law. The fitted exponent kk is close to zero, so the fitted function is effectively equivalent to a logarithmic curve. The logarithmic form produces a poorer fit than the saturating exponential on every trajectory.: a power law L=a​Cp+L0L=aC^{p}+L_{0}, the simplest unbounded form, and a saturating exponential L=Lmax​(1−exp⁡(−(C/C0)k))L=L_{\max}\bigl(1-\exp\bigl(-(C/C_{0})^{k}\bigr)\bigr), the simplest bounded form, with a ceiling LmaxL_{\max}.

Under the constraint L0≥0L_{0}\geq 0 (to ensure positive lookahead) the fitted offset vanishes, leaving a pure power law. Table 2 gives the fitted forms and their in-sample RMSE.

The saturating exponential achieves lower in-sample RMSE than the power law by factors of 2.72.7 and 5.65.6 on Qwen3-0.6B and Pythia-1.4B, respectively.

We next test whether this in-sample advantage extends to prediction. We fit both forms on the first 70%70\% of each trajectory’s stage completions, ordered by cumulative compute, and evaluate on the remaining 30%30\%. Held-out RMSE is 1.4×1.4\times and 23.8×23.8\times lower for the saturating exponential on Qwen3-0.6B and Pythia-1.4B (Table 3). A Diebold–Mariano test (Diebold and Mariano, 1995) is a standard comparison of held-out forecast errors. Because errors along a single trajectory are serially correlated, however, we instead apply the test to the number of training iterations required to complete each stage, whose residuals are approximately independent (Appendix D.1). On both trajectories, the saturating exponential predicts the held-out duration of each stage significantly better than the power law (p=7×10−10p=7{\times}10^{-10} for Qwen3-0.6B and p=1.5×10−4p=1.5{\times}10^{-4} for Pythia-1.4B; Table 3). The advantage also increases with lookahead, as the gap between the two forms’ held-out prediction errors widens at later stages. Appendix D reports the results of the same comparisons on Pythia-410M and Pythia-2.8B.

Within our observed range both forms describe the data closely, but achieved LL decelerates faster than a power law allows. The saturating fit is better, and it assigns each model a finite ceiling LmaxL_{\max}. The slowdown is particularly pronounced for Pythia-1.4B. Within a budget of 5M PFLOPs, it reaches L=75L{=}75, 91%91\% of the fitted asymptote Lmax≈82L_{\max}\approx 82. Its last five completed stages, L=71L{=}71–7575, consume 2.102.10M PFLOPs, approximately 42%42\% of the budget, and the per-stage cost is still increasing at the end of training (Appendix D.2, Figure 12).

These trajectories suggest a model- and procedure-specific ceiling on achievable lookahead: for a given model, our curriculum appears to drive LL upward with diminishing returns toward that ceiling.

4.3 Small Step Sizes Are Required for Deep Curriculum Progression

Our curriculum has one main hyperparameter, the step size ss, which controls the increase in maximum lookahead LL between consecutive stages. We examine how ss affects the lookahead the curriculum reaches within a fixed compute budget. We tune Qwen3-0.6B using our curriculum at step sizes s∈{1,4,8,16,32,64}s\in\{1,4,8,16,32,64\}, each with a target lookahead of L=256L{=}256.

Figure 5 shows that the step size must be neither too large nor too small. A step size that is too large stalls curriculum advancement: s=64s{=}64 stalls at L=128L{=}128 and s=32s{=}32 at L=192L{=}192. A step size that is too small does not stall but advances slowly: within 300K PFLOPs, s=1s{=}1 reaches only L=145L{=}145 and s=4s{=}4 reaches L=212L{=}212, whereas s=8s{=}8 and s=16s{=}16 achieves the target of L=256L{=}256. A plausible explanation for stalling is that larger ss makes training more similar to the no-curriculum case: at ss equal to the target lookahead the curriculum has a single stage, which is exactly the no-curriculum case, and Section 4.1 shows that this stalls at L=256L{=}256. The higher the target, the smaller ss must be to avoid stalling.

4.4 Maximum Intrinsic Lookahead Grows with Model Scale

Prior work finds that scaling model size alone does not improve implicit reasoning (Saparov et al., 2025). We test whether this conclusion holds with curriculum learning, and whether the curriculum’s progression rate depends on model size. We train Pythia models of four different sizes (160M, 410M, 1.4B, 2.8B) using our curriculum with s=1s=1, with learning rate and batch size individually tuned per model size (Appendix B).

At matched compute, larger models reach greater lookaheads once the training budget is sufficiently large (Figure 6). Pythia-2.8B achieves the deepest lookahead among the tested Pythia models (L=133L{=}133). It completes L=130L{=}130 using 2.40M PFLOPs, less than half the compute Pythia-1.4B uses to reach L=75L{=}75 (4.97M PFLOPs). Pythia-160M plateaus at L=9L{=}9 over the observed trajectory, suggesting that the model’s capacity is insufficient for curriculum progression.

Scaling of the fitted asymptote with model size.

The saturating exponential’s asymptote LmaxL_{\max} is itself model-dependent. We fit the saturating-exponential curve introduced in Section 4.2 separately to each Pythia trajectory except that of Pythia-160M, which plateaus at L=9L{=}9. The fitted asymptote rises with model size: Lmax≈51L_{\max}\approx 51, 8282, and 235235 for Pythia-410M, -1.4B, and -2.8B respectively (per-size fits in Appendix D, Figure 11; fitted parameters in Table 19). Parameter count is not the whole story, however: Qwen3-0.6B has a fitted asymptote of Lmax≈324L_{\max}{\approx}324, well above the larger Pythia-1.4B’s ≈82{\approx}82, suggesting that factors beyond parameter count also affect a model’s maximum intrinsic lookahead. Bootstrap intervals (Table 19) show that the ordering of these ceilings is robust.

4.5 Pretrained Initialization Reaches Greater Lookahead at Matched Compute

Lee et al. (2025) report that pretrained initialization accelerates curriculum progression in arithmetic and maze-solving tasks. We test whether this effect holds for our curriculum learning in reasoning and quantify the size of the gap. We train Pythia-1.4B and Qwen3-0.6B, each twice under our curriculum with s=1s{=}1: once from the released pretrained checkpoint (full fine-tuning) and once from random weights (training from scratch). Learning rate and batch size are tuned separately for each condition, since random initialization makes little progress under the small learning rate suited to fine-tuning (Appendix B). Pretraining gives a large head start in both families (Figure 7). Within a budget of 1.5M PFLOPs, random initialization reaches L=23L{=}23 for Pythia-1.4B and L=35L{=}35 for Qwen3-0.6B. Pretrained initialization reaches the same lookaheads with ∼53×{\sim}53\times and ∼117×{\sim}117\times less compute, respectively (Table 14, Appendix C.4). That the stronger, more heavily pretrained model benefits more suggests the curriculum builds on capabilities already present in the pretrained weights rather than instilling them from scratch. Applying our curriculum to Pythia-1.4B checkpoints saved after different amounts of pretraining shows the same pattern within a single model, as checkpoints with more pretraining need less compute to advance through the curriculum (Appendix C.4).

Pretrained models have a larger fitted asymptote.

We train the randomly initialized Qwen3-0.6B long enough to fit the curve of Section 4.2, which gives Lmax≈120L_{\max}\approx 120, against ≈324\approx 324 from pretrained initialization. This suggests that without pretrained knowledge, the model not only progresses more slowly but also reaches a lower ceiling.

4.6 Implicit Reasoning Learned on Synthetic Data Transfers Downstream

We now ask whether the implicit-reasoning capability acquired through curriculum learning on synthetic data transfers to natural language reasoning benchmarks. We fine-tune Qwen3-1.7B with our curriculum (s=1s=1). To avoid catastrophic forgetting of the instruction-following capability that downstream benchmarks require, we draw 6% of training examples, outside the curriculum, from the instruction-tuning corpus Dolci-Instruct-SFT (Olmo Team, 2025).

We evaluate at curriculum stages L∈{8,16,32,48}L\in\{8,16,32,48\} on 14 downstream reasoning tasks spanning logical, multi-hop, constraint-satisfaction, and graph reasoning (Tafjord et al., 2021; Clark et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2025a; Saparov et al., 2023; Han et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025; Qi et al., 2025; Sinha et al., 2019; Parmar et al., 2024; Suzgun et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2020; Zhong et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023a) (full list in Table 4; descriptions in Appendix G). Evaluating at multiple stages tracks how the transfer evolves as the curriculum deepens. We compare against the same model trained without curriculum, directly at L=48L{=}48, compute-matched to the final curriculum checkpoint.

Table 4 reports the results, and Appendix F additionally reports the base model and an instruction-only control. At L=48L{=}48, training with curriculum outperforms training without curriculum on 11 of the 14 benchmarks, with statistically significant gains on ProofWriter (both settings), JustLogic, ZebraLogic-MC, PrOntoQA, ParaRules, FOLIO, and LogicBench-BQA. On the three benchmarks where the model trained without curriculum scores higher, none of the differences is significant. These results suggest that training a model with curriculum learning to perform long-horizon implicit reasoning can improve its downstream reasoning. Optimizing the training procedure to maximize these gains is left to future work.

General model capability is preserved.

On eight language-understanding benchmarks and IFEval, the curriculum-trained Qwen3-1.7B exceeds the non-finetuned model at every curriculum stage (eight-benchmark mean ranging from 63.4 to 64.2 for the various curriculum approaches vs. 61.7 for non-finetuned model) and stays within one point of a compute-matched model fine-tuned only on instruction data (Table 24, Appendix F.1). Thus, we find no evidence that gains in implicit reasoning come at the expense of general capability.

5 Conclusion

We investigate whether LLMs can be trained to perform implicit reasoning at greater depths using a curriculum over lookahead and attribute vocabulary size that gradually increases the maximum number of steps the model must search ahead to identify the next step in a proof. We find that curriculum learning enables models to reach greater depths than no-curriculum baselines. Achieved lookahead grows predictably with training compute but decelerates and fine-tuning progresses, and across both model families, the trajectories are better described by a saturating exponential than by an unbounded power law, suggesting a maximum intrinsic lookahead that varies across models. Our fits suggest that model size and pretrained initialization raise the maximum intrinsic lookahead, while step sizes that are too large cause the curriculum to stall. Finally, the capability acquired on synthetic data can transfer to downstream natural-language reasoning benchmarks, showing that curriculum-trained implicit reasoning can generalize beyond the synthetic training distribution.

Future work includes separating the effects of architecture and pretraining on the fitted asymptotes, applying the curriculum to semantically richer generators with a controllable difficulty parameter, and training curriculum-trained models with reinforcement learning to measure the effect on chain-of-thought length and backtracking.

Reproducibility Statement

All required details to reproduce our results are contained in the paper and its appendices. Additionally, our full code is freely available at https://github.com/MaxNickell/implicit-reasoning-curriculum. The task formulation and the curriculum over lookahead and attribute vocabulary are specified in Sections 3.1 and 3.2; the training procedure is given as pseudocode in Appendix A, and worked examples of generated training instances appear in Appendix H. Training data is produced with a modified version of the DeepRD generator, with our modifications described in Section 3.1. Model configurations, optimizer settings, batch sizes, and learning rates for every experiment are listed in Appendix B. The downstream evaluation protocol, including benchmarks, prompting format, and scoring, is given in Appendices E and G; all models are evaluated under an identical protocol. Confidence intervals and the significance tests behind our downstream comparisons are reported in Appendix F, and the curve-fitting procedure behind our L⁡(C)L(C) claims, including held-out validation, is detailed in Appendix D. We note that every downstream number comes from a single training seed, and that the intervals we report reflect evaluation sampling only.

Appendix A Curriculum Training Algorithm

The pseudocode below specifies the curriculum training procedure described in Section 3.2. Stages advance based on a rolling exact-match accuracy criterion over the WW most recent training examples, after a per-stage minimum step floor (200 steps, see Appendix B) is reached.

Appendix B Experimental Details

We list the training hyperparameters for each experiment in Section 4. All experiments use AdamW (β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9, β2=0.999\beta_{2}=0.999, ϵ=10−8\epsilon=10^{-8}) with a constant learning rate, no weight decay, gradient clipping at 1.01.0, and bf16 mixed precision; we find scheduled learning rates consistently degrade or fail to improve over constant LR. All experiments use a fixed random seed of 12341234. Unless noted, every experiment uses 100 warmup steps, τ=0.98\tau=0.98 rolling-accuracy advancement threshold over a rolling window of W=800W=800 examples, and a 200-step floor per stage. Training uses predominantly 2–4×\times NVIDIA H100 80GB GPUs, with 8×\times NVIDIA H200 used for Pythia-2.8B and 6×\times NVIDIA A100 80GB used for Pythia-160M and parts of the Qwen3-1.7B downstream training. Gradient accumulation is chosen to match the effective batch size listed per experiment. Downstream evaluation uses a single NVIDIA A100 GPU.

Notation.

“Batch size” refers to the combined effective batch size across GPUs. All Pythia and Qwen3 models are initialized from the released checkpoints (Pythia: base; Qwen3: the post-trained release) unless explicitly marked random init.

B.1 Joint Curriculum vs. Fixed-Vocabulary (Section 4.1)

Both configurations use Qwen3-0.6B (full FT) with the same optimization stack as Section 4.1: batch 768, LR 5×10−55\times 10^{-5}, curriculum step s=8s=8 to L=256L{=}256. They differ only in attribute-vocabulary handling: the joint configuration scales the attribute vocabulary size with stage as |𝒱k|=2​(Lk+1)|\mathcal{V}_{k}|=2(L_{k}+1), while the fixed-vocabulary configuration holds |𝒱||\mathcal{V}| at the maximum from the start. The runs with |𝒱k|=b​Lk+2|\mathcal{V}_{k}|=bL_{k}+2 for b∈{3,4}b\in\{3,4\} use the same settings.

B.2 Curriculum vs. No-Curriculum (Section 4.1)

B.3 Scaling Behavior (Section 4.2)

Qwen3-0.6B uses batch 768 and LR 5×10−55\times 10^{-5} with s=1s=1 and a target of L=256L{=}256; Pythia-1.4B uses the per-model settings in Table 6 with s=1s=1 and a target of L=96L{=}96.

B.4 Curriculum Step Size Sweep (Section 4.3)

All six step sizes share the same Qwen3-0.6B optimization stack: batch 768, LR 5×10−55\times 10^{-5}, curriculum to L=256L{=}256.

B.5 Model Size Sweep (Section 4.4)

Batch size and learning rate are tuned per model size by a small grid search; for each model, we select the (batch size, learning rate) pair that produces the fastest curriculum advancement during early stages.

B.6 Initialization (Section 4.5)

Random initialization makes little progress under the small learning rate suited to fine-tuning, so each condition uses its own best-found learning rate and batch size.

B.7 Downstream Reasoning Transfer (Section 4.6)

Qwen3-1.7B uses a 6% Dolci-Instruct-SFT mix-in alongside the graph-search curriculum; the matched-compute baseline trains the same model on the same mix without curriculum, directly at L=48L{=}48. The instruction-only control trains the same model with the same optimizer settings on 100% Dolci-Instruct-SFT, with no graph-search data. All three configurations wrap inputs in a chat template with enable_thinking=False.

Intermediate pretraining checkpoints.

We test whether the benefit grows with the amount of pretraining within a single model. We fine-tune Pythia-1.4B from three intermediate checkpoints released by Biderman et al. (2023), at pretraining steps 1,000, 10,000 and 100,000 (about 2.1B, 21B and 210B tokens). Each trajectory follows the curriculum with s=1s{=}1, using the pretrained Pythia-1.4B batch size and learning rate (192 and 2.7×10−52.7\times 10^{-5}) with no warmup, and stops at 500K PFLOPs. Later checkpoints advance faster (Figure 10, Table 15). The step-100,000 checkpoint completes L=24L{=}24 with about 9×9\times less compute than the step-1,000 checkpoint and reaches L=57L{=}57 within the budget, while both earlier checkpoints stop at L=27L{=}27. The advantage of step 10,000 over step 1,000 shrinks as LL grows, while the advantage of step 100,000 over step 10,000 widens. Even the step-1,000 checkpoint completes L=8L{=}8 with about 8×8\times less compute than random initialization.

C.5 LoRA vs. Full Fine-Tuning

We compare full fine-tuning, used in all other experiments, with LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) at ranks r=8r{=}8 and r=64r{=}64. All three conditions train Qwen3-0.6B under the curriculum with s=8s{=}8 up to L=128L{=}128, using the step-size sweep settings of Appendix B without warmup. Adapters are applied to all attention and MLP projections, with α=2​r\alpha{=}2r and dropout 0.1. Because the frozen base weights need no weight gradients, we count LoRA compute as 4​N+6​NLoRA4N+6N_{\text{LoRA}} per token, where NLoRAN_{\text{LoRA}} is the number of adapter parameters. Both ranks reach L=128L{=}128 with roughly the same compute as full fine-tuning (0.95×0.95\times for r=8r{=}8 and 0.85×0.85\times for r=64r{=}64) but need more optimizer steps (1.56×1.56\times and 1.13×1.13\times; Table 16). Each condition uses a single seed, so these ratios are approximate. We use full fine-tuning elsewhere because it reaches the same lookahead with similar compute and does not require choosing a LoRA rank.

Appendix D Functional forms for achieved lookahead

We fit achieved lookahead LL as a function of cumulative training compute CC for the two trajectories of Section 4.2, Qwen3-0.6B and Pythia-1.4B, and for the less trained Pythia-410M and Pythia-2.8B, using the power law and saturating exponential defined there. This appendix reports the full comparison (RMSE with confidence intervals, AICc, and held-out prediction of both cumulative lookahead and per-stage training iterations), along with the per-size saturating exponential fits underlying the ceiling analysis of Section 4.2 (Figure 11).

Data and procedure.

Stage completions (one point per stage, L∈[1,Lend]L\in[1,L_{\text{end}}], at the compute where the 98%98\% gate is passed) yield n=244n=244 points for Qwen3-0.6B and n=46n=46, 7575 and 133133 for Pythia-410M, -1.4B and -2.8B. We fit each form with SciPy differential_evolution (Sobol init, popsize=30, maxiter=200, seed=42) polished by Levenberg–Marquardt, retaining the lowest-RSS solution. Confidence intervals on RMSE are 95% moving-block bootstrap intervals (block length ≈n1/3{\approx}\,n^{1/3}, 300–500 resamples), which partly account for the serial correlation of a single trajectory; with residual autocorrelation persisting over many lags they should be read as descriptive, not as calibrated 95% intervals. Δ\DeltaAICc treats the stage points as independent, which they are not (residual autocorrelation exceeds 0.80.8 at lag 1), so we read it as a ranking of in-sample fit rather than as a calibrated test; the formal comparison is the held-out test on per-stage training iterations in Appendix D.1. Because the power-law offset is at its bound L0=0L_{0}=0 in every fit and the saturating exponential approaches a​CkaC^{k} as C0C_{0} grows, the in-sample comparison is one-sided by construction and only the size of the RMSE gap is informative. Held-out comparisons fit both forms on the first 70%70\% of the stage points, ordered by compute, and evaluate their predictions on the remainder (Table 17).

What the comparison shows.

On every trajectory the saturating exponential attains lower RMSE, is preferred by AICc (Δ​AICc=57\Delta\text{AICc}=57–493493; Table 18) and predicts the held-out stages with lower RMSE (Table 17). The in-sample gap is largest on the three trajectories nearest their fitted ceilings and small on Pythia-2.8B (RMSE 2.672.67 vs. 2.152.15), which sits at only ∼57%{\sim}57\% of its fitted ceiling and whose RMSE intervals overlap; the two forms separate more cleanly as a model nears its ceiling. Appendix D.1 reports a significance test on per-stage training iterations. Figure 11 plots the per-size saturating exponential fits (parameters in Table 19); the resulting ceilings (Lmax≈51L_{\max}\approx 51, 8282, 235235) underlie the ceiling analysis in Section 4.2. The bootstrap intervals in Table 19 show that the lower bound of each ceiling is well determined, while the upper bound is poorly determined for the two trajectories furthest from saturation, Qwen3-0.6B and Pythia-2.8B. Pythia-160M plateaus at L=9L{=}9 (Section 4.4) and is excluded, since neither form is meaningful for a capacity-limited trajectory.

D.1 Held-out prediction of per-stage training iterations

A Diebold–Mariano test on the held-out residuals of L⁡(C)L(C) is not valid for these trajectories. Its variance estimate assumes a weakly dependent loss differential, whereas the held-out residuals along a single trajectory share one extrapolation error and are strongly autocorrelated (lag-1 autocorrelation 0.950.95 for Qwen3-0.6B and 0.920.92 for Pythia-2.8B; Table 20). We therefore compare the two forms on a quantity whose residuals are approximately independent, the number of training iterations required to complete each stage, Δ​I​(L)=I⁡(L)−I⁡(L−1)\Delta I(L)=I(L)-I(L-1) with I⁡(0)=0I(0)=0, where I⁡(L)I(L) is the cumulative number of optimizer steps at the completion of stage LL. We use iterations rather than compute because the compute cost of a stage is its iteration count multiplied by the tokens per step, and tokens per step grow with LL as the sequence length grows, so per-stage iterations isolate the learning dynamics from that growth. Each form implies a per-stage iteration count g⁡(L)−g⁡(L−1)g(L)-g(L-1), where gg is the inverse of the form fitted with cumulative iterations as the independent variable. We fit both forms to log⁡Δ​I​(L)\log\Delta I(L) by least squares on the first 70%70\% of stages, ordered by compute, and predict the remaining stages. Table 20 shows that on per-stage iterations the residuals of the saturating exponential are consistent with independence on three trajectories and marginal on Pythia-1.4B (p=0.046p=0.046).

For each held-out stage we form the loss differential dL=ePL​(L)2−eSE​(L)2d_{L}=e_{\mathrm{PL}}(L)^{2}-e_{\mathrm{SE}}(L)^{2} in log units, which is positive when the saturating exponential predicts that stage better. Because the advantage may grow with depth, we regress dLd_{L} on the centered stage index with Newey–West standard errors (Bartlett kernel, bandwidth ⌊4​(T/100)2/9⌋\lfloor 4(T/100)^{2/9}\rfloor) and report the intercept α\alpha, which equals the mean of dLd_{L}, and the slope β\beta (Table 21). All pp-values are two-sided and are stable for bandwidths from 00 to four times this rule. The saturating exponential has lower held-out RMSE on per-stage iterations for three trajectories and ties on Pythia-2.8B. The advantage is significant for Qwen3-0.6B, Pythia-410M and Pythia-1.4B, and on all three it grows with depth (β>0\beta>0). Across train/held-out splits from 50%50\% to 80%80\% of the stages, α\alpha is significant at every split for Qwen3-0.6B and Pythia-410M, at the 70%70\% split only for Pythia-1.4B, and at no split for Pythia-2.8B. The Pythia-1.4B result is sensitive to the split because that trajectory’s per-stage costs vary by two orders of magnitude between adjacent stages, so a held-out set of 88 to 2424 stages is dominated by a few of them. For Pythia-2.8B the two forms predict per-stage iterations identically, because the saturating exponential fitted to that trajectory’s iterations has no identified ceiling and reduces to the power law. Per-stage iterations are a noisy quantity, with held-out RMSE near 11 in log units for both forms, so this test has less power than the comparison on cumulative lookahead but rests on assumptions the data satisfy.

D.2 Compute per curriculum stage

Figure 12 shows the mean compute per completed curriculum stage for Pythia-1.4B with s=1s=1, averaged over consecutive groups of five stages. The last five completed stages, L=71L{=}71–7575, consume 2.102.10M PFLOPs, approximately 42%42\% of its 5M-PFLOP budget. Thus, nearly half the training compute produces only five additional stages of progress, illustrating the sharply diminishing returns to further training in this regime. Within this budget, the trajectory reaches L=75L{=}75, 91%91\% of the fitted asymptote Lmax≈82L_{\max}\approx 82, without having plateaued. The flattening captured by the saturating exponential is therefore accompanied by a substantial observed increase in the compute required for further curriculum progress.

Appendix E Downstream Evaluation Methodology

Next-step proof prediction.

On the synthetic next-step prediction task (Section 3.1) we use greedy autoregressive decoding, and the first whitespace- or punctuation-delimited word of the generated continuation is compared case-insensitively with any accepted gold attribute.

We evaluate on 14 reasoning benchmarks (full list in Table 4). Thirteen are scored by log-likelihood over a fixed candidate label set; the open-ended NLGraph benchmark uses its authors’ per-task scorers. Samples are drawn with a fixed random seed, and the number of items per benchmark is listed in Table 25.

Why constrained log-likelihood rather than CoT.

Several of these benchmarks are designed for chain-of-thought or free-form decoding. Our curriculum-trained models do not produce verbose CoT natively. The curriculum task contains no signal for natural-language reasoning style, so unconstrained free-form decoding would entangle output style with underlying capability. For benchmarks with a fixed answer set we therefore use log-likelihood scoring over the candidate labels, isolating reasoning from format-following. This is the same convention used by lm-evaluation-harness (Gao et al., 2026) for its loglikelihood request type.

Fused single-pass scoring.

For each example we run the model once on the prompt and compute the per-token log-probabilities of every candidate label. When a label tokenizes to a single token (the common case for True/False/Unknown, multiple-choice letters, etc.) we read its log-prob directly from the next-token distribution. For multi-token labels we fall back to teacher-forced log-likelihood with the same approach as lm-evaluation-harness: walk forward to the first divergent token between tokenize⁡(prefix)\mathrm{tokenize}(\text{prefix}) and tokenize⁡(prefix+label)\mathrm{tokenize}(\text{prefix}+\text{label}), then sum log-probs of the suffix tokens. This handles BPE boundary merges correctly and remains a single forward pass per choice.

Reported metric.

The headline accuracy reported in Table 4 is log-likelihood accuracy: argmax over candidate labels by total log-probability. This matches the dominant convention for log-likelihood-scored benchmarks in the literature.

Per-benchmark prompting protocol.

For each benchmark we adapt its canonical LLM evaluation protocol to a constrained-log-likelihood setting: we keep the canonical demonstration count and prompt format where compatible, and substitute Direct prompting where the canonical convention uses chain-of-thought. The same protocol is applied to the base model, every curriculum checkpoint, the no-curriculum baseline, and the instruction-only control for each benchmark. Per-benchmark choices are summarized in Table 22.

Sampling and stratification.

Item counts per benchmark are listed in Table 25. For benchmarks with subsets (per-depth, per-task, or per-puzzle-size), we draw a fixed-seed random sample within each subset rather than a deterministic prefix. ProofWriter OWA and ParaRules are label-balanced within each depth; PrOntoQA and Web of Lies use 500 items per depth; NLGraph uses 125 items per sub-task.

NLGraph (generation).

NLGraph contains 8 sub-tasks (shortest path, Hamilton, connectivity, etc.) and the canonical scoring is per-task: path validation for Hamilton, weight match for shortest path, regex-based answer extraction for others. We use the authors’ canonical k-shot-prompt.txt files (with task-dependent kk, no CoT) and their per-task scorers ported from the official repo. The accuracy we report on NLGraph is the average of these per-task scores.

Appendix F Confidence Intervals on Downstream Results

Table 23 reports the accuracies of Table 4 with 95% confidence intervals, together with the base model and the instruction-only control, and marks every curriculum checkpoint that is significantly above training without curriculum, not only the best one per benchmark. The base model and the instruction-only control are not part of the matched comparison, and they score above curriculum L=48L{=}48 on four and six of the 14 benchmarks, respectively.

F.1 General model capability

Table 24 reports the accuracies summarized in Section 4.6. The benchmarks are MMLU, ARC-Easy and ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, PIQA, BoolQ, LAMBADA and IFEval. Each is evaluated on the non-finetuned Qwen3-1.7B, on an instruction-only control, on the model trained without curriculum, and on four curriculum stage checkpoints. The first eight benchmarks probe knowledge and single-step commonsense rather than multi-step deductive chaining, so we do not expect the curriculum to improve them.

Because the curriculum trains the model almost exclusively on synthetic proof data, it could plausibly narrow the capabilities of the model in other respects. We evaluate Qwen3-1.7B on 8 standard benchmarks spanning world knowledge (MMLU), science QA (ARC-Easy/Challenge), commonsense inference (HellaSwag, WinoGrande, PIQA), reading comprehension (BoolQ) and discourse-level language modeling (LAMBADA), plus IFEval for instruction following, using an identical lm-evaluation-harness protocol for every model evaluated. Mean accuracy over the eight is above the non-finetuned model’s at every curriculum stage (63.4 to 64.2 vs. 61.7; Table 24). The largest single-benchmark drop below it is WinoGrande at L=48L{=}48 (59.8 vs. 61.7). IFEval is also above the non-finetuned model at every stage (34.6 to 41.2 vs. 33.1). Because our training mixture also contains instruction data, a comparison against the non-finetuned model alone would leave open the possibility that this instruction data offsets damage done by the synthetic data. We therefore fine-tune the same base model on 100% Dolci-Instruct-SFT, with no synthetic data and no curriculum but otherwise identical hyperparameters, and evaluate it at cumulative training compute matched to the L=48L{=}48 curriculum checkpoint. It scores within one point of that checkpoint on the eight-benchmark mean (64.2 vs. 63.4), so training on the synthetic data adds little measurable cost on these benchmarks. The model trained without curriculum on the same data at the same compute scores essentially the same as the curriculum (63.2), so the curriculum itself adds no further cost. On IFEval, the L=48L{=}48 checkpoint scores below the instruction-only control (41.2 vs. 46.4), which trains on instruction data alone, and slightly above the model trained without curriculum (40.1). Thus, we find no evidence that gains in implicit reasoning capability are at the expense of general model capability.

Appendix G Benchmark Descriptions

Table 25 summarizes the fourteen downstream reasoning benchmarks and the nine general-capability benchmarks: the reasoning type each targets, the answer format we score, the split or subset we evaluate, and the number of evaluation items nn. The prompting protocol for each benchmark is given in Table 22.

PrOntoQA.

The released PrOntoQA data stops at 4 to 5 hops, and the shipped generator cannot go further, because it samples a random ontology over 17 concept names and takes a random proof walk through it. We replace the ontology sampler with a chain of exactly k+1k+1 concepts, script the walk to the unique kk-step proof, and enlarge the vocabulary to 624 names and 274 adjectives. Rendering, inflection, parsing, distractors and label negation use the official code. An independent solver verifies every item for its label, for a proof depth equal to kk, for consistency, and for distractor sign. The set covers eight depths, k∈{1,2,4,8,16,32,48,64}k\in\{1,2,4,8,16,32,48,64\}, 500 items each, balanced on both the label and the query polarity.

ProofWriter OWA and ParaRules.

We use the published data but draw equal numbers of True, False and Unknown items within each official QDep stratum. Without this, the Unknown share falls from 69% at depth 0 to 3% at depth 5, because an unprovable question inherits the depth of its deepest failing search, so a model that always answers Unknown would score 66% at depth 0 and 4% at depth 5. Balancing fixes chance at 33.3% at every depth. The closed-world split is already near 50/50 at every depth and needs no resampling. We apply the same balancing to ParaRules, whose items come from the ProofWriter open-world NatLang test split.

Web of Lies.

Our Web of Lies set is generated from the BBH web_of_lies template and its 50-name pool, as truth-value chains of k∈{1,2,4,8,16,32,48,64}k\in\{1,2,4,8,16,32,48,64\} speakers with 500 items per depth and exactly balanced Yes/No labels. Our solver reproduces all 250 published BBH items, all of which have k=4k{=}4.

All other benchmarks are the published data as released. Source repositories: ProofWriter from AllenAI proofwriter-dataset-V2020.12.3; FOLIO from yale-nlp/FOLIO; ZebraLogic from WildEval/ZebraLogic; RuleTaker from tasksource/ruletaker (fallback hitachi-nlp/ruletaker); CLUTRR from kendrivp/CLUTRR_v1_extracted (fallback kliang5/CLUTRR_huggingface_dataset); LogiQA from Zhong et al. (2023); LogicBench and NLGraph from their authors’ releases.

We show generated training examples at three lookahead values to illustrate how problem complexity scales across curriculum stages.
